limitations: All results are on SYNTHETIC data whose clean trip loads follow Benford's Law exactly by construction. They show the detectors work IF genuine data behaves like this; whether real Indian municipal tonnage data conforms is untested here (Phase 1 item 6). Section [8a] shows the Benford-reference check would flag most clean wards if genuine trip loads were only approximately Benford.

Tamper models (1-sig-fig rounding, uniform fabrication over the ward's P10-P90, multiplicative inflation) are assumptions about how fraud looks, not observed fraud patterns. A fabricator who draws values from a Benford-like distribution, or inflates by small amounts, would evade the digit tests; only the baseline layer constrains that, and only for large over-reporting.

The baseline model uses the generator's own log-linear functional form, so it partly recovers the generator by construction. Its sensitivity is set by the unexplained ward heterogeneity (synthetic ward_effect_sigma); see section [8b]. On real data that spread is unknown.
The roundness test compares each ward with the other wards; if every ward rounds the same way it cannot see it. The peer-reference digit test has the same blind spot.
Detection is evaluated at ward level (the unit that holds or releases credits). Entry-level and ward-day localisation hints are emitted for flagged wards but their precision is not evaluated here.
confidence_score is the smallest BH-adjusted p-value across checks: a ranking of evidence, not a probability that a ward's data is genuine.
The implied per-capita generation of the synthetic city is an artefact of synthetic populations and must not be quoted.
